exam: What bedside investigation confirms IVH in a 28‑week neonate? — Cranial ultrasound through the anterior fontanelle; it is rapid, bedside, and shows ventricular echogenicity.
A pre‑term infant develops a bulging fontanelle on day 3. What is your next step? — Obtain an urgent cranial ultrasound to assess for IVH and ventricular size.
How does the Papile grade influence prognosis? — Higher grades (III‑IV) are associated with increased risk of hydrocephalus and neuro‑developmental impairment.
Why should aggressive fluid boluses be avoided in suspected IVH? — They can raise cerebral venous pressure, worsening bleeding.
What coagulation abnormality is most relevant in IVH and how is it treated? — Vitamin K‑dependent factor deficiency; give vitamin K and, if severe, fresh frozen plasma.
Distinguish post‑hemorrhagic hydrocephalus from ongoing IVH on imaging. — Hydrocephalus shows enlarged ventricles without fresh echogenic blood; ongoing IVH shows new intraventricular echoes.
Why is phenobarbital preferred for seizures in IVH over benzodiazepines? — It has less effect on platelet function and is effective for neonatal seizures.
What preventive measure given antenatally reduces IVH risk and why? — Antenatal corticosteroids mature the germinal matrix vessels, decreasing fragility.
ai.title: Intraventricular Haemorrhage in the Neonate
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH) is bleeding into the brain's ventricular system, mainly affecting pre‑term infants. Early recognition, appropriate imaging and supportive care reduce mortality and long‑term neuro‑disability.

b: Cranial US: bedside, no radiation, shows echogenic material in ventricles
CT/MRI: confirm extent when US equivocal or for surgical planning
sections.p: IVH is bleeding into the lateral ventricles, usually originating from the fragile germinal matrix in pre‑term neonates. Diagnosis is made by cranial ultrasound through the anterior fontanelle, or by CT/MRI if needed.

b: Grade I: sub‑ependymal germinal matrix haemorrhage only
Grade II: IVH without ventricular dilatation
Grade III: IVH with ventricular dilatation
Grade IV: IVH with parenchymal haemorrhagic infarction
sections.p: The Papile grading system (modified by Volpe) is used to stage IVH and guide prognosis.

b: Prematurity (<32 weeks gestation) – most common
Birth asphyxia / hypoxic‑ischemic injury
Rapid volume shifts (e.g., aggressive fluid resuscitation)
Coagulopathy (maternal or neonatal)
Infection (sepsis, meningitis) – especially in low‑resource settings
sections.p: Bleeding results from rupture of fragile vessels in the germinal matrix under rapid fluctuations in cerebral blood flow.

b: Apnea or bradycardia episodes
Fluctuating tone, seizures, or irritability
Bulging fontanelle, increasing head circumference
Post‑hemorrhagic hydrocephalus signs: sunset eyes, vomiting
sections.p: Early IVH may be silent; later grades produce neurological signs as ventricles enlarge.

t.b: Confirms presence and grade of IVH; guides monitoring
Detects anemia, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy that may worsen bleeding
Identifies metabolic contributors to seizures or worsening edema

b: Progressive ventricular dilatation → post‑hemorrhagic hydrocephalus
Periventricular leukomalacia
Seizures refractory to medication
Severe anemia or coagulopathy
sections.p: Complications can be rapidly fatal or cause long‑term disability.

b: Maintain stable cerebral perfusion: avoid rapid BP swings, use gentle fluid boluses
Correct coagulopathy: give vitamin K, platelets, or fresh frozen plasma as indicated
Treat anaemia: packed red cells if Hb < 8 g/dL and symptomatic
Control seizures: phenobarbital first line, avoid drugs that lower platelet function
If hydrocephalus develops, consider ventricular drainage or shunt (surgical referral)
sections.p: Treatment focuses on stabilising the infant, preventing expansion, and addressing complications.

b: Serial cranial US every 1–2 weeks until discharge
Neuro‑developmental assessment at 6 months, 12 months, then yearly
Preventive measures: antenatal steroids, gentle ventilation, delayed cord clamping, meticulous handling of pre‑term infants
sections.p: Survivors need neuro‑developmental monitoring and imaging to detect delayed hydrocephalus.
